strengths: Novel and compelling problem formulation: While worldwide image geolocation is well-studied, global-scale audio geolocation—specifically leveraging natural and wildlife acoustics—is an underexplored, challenging, and ecologically meaningful direction.

Comprehensive benchmarking of diverse paradigms: The paper thoroughly formalizes and benchmarks multiple fundamental approaches, including coordinate regression (Euclidean and Haversine), hierarchical spatial classification (H3 hexagonal bins), explicit species range integration (via SINR), and contrastive retrieval.

Insightful ecological grounding and upper-bound analysis: The use of species checklists and range maps provides a clear theoretical foundation. Evaluating 'species oracles' under varying levels of corruption clearly demonstrates the theoretical ceiling of species-based geolocation.

Extensive experimental analysis: The authors provide detailed ablations on audio encoders, location encoders, aggregation methods, gallery construction, as well as new test scenarios such as spatiotemporal neighborhood aggregation and dawn chorus soundscapes (XCDC).

Creative qualitative demonstrations: The application to multimodal geo-forensics (identifying soundstage/foley discrepancies in Hollywood films) and cross-modal retrieval (audio to text/flags) effectively illustrates the practical relevance and potential of joint audio-location embeddings.
weaknesses: Fairness in audio encoder comparisons: In Table 2(a), the off-the-shelf audio foundation models (CLAP, Wav2CLIP) are evaluated without fine-tuning (FT = ✗), whereas MobileNet-V3 is fine-tuned (FT = ✓). A fine-tuned native audio backbone (or bioacoustic transformer such as BEATs or AST) would provide a fairer and more conclusive assessment of audio representation capacity.

Dependence on retrieval gallery distribution: As shown in Table A1, performance is sensitive to the choice of location gallery. City-scale accuracy drops sharply from 6.6% (using training coordinates) to 1.3% (uniform 1° grid), indicating that retrieval against training points may benefit from training set spatial clustering/density bias.

Low fine-scale accuracy and difficulty generalizing to complex soundscapes: The model achieves only 6.4% at the city scale (25 km) on iNatSounds and drops to 4.3% at the region scale (200 km) on the multi-species XCDC dataset, highlighting that decomposing dense, overlapping acoustic environments remains an open challenge.

strengths: Pioneering formulation and benchmarking of global-scale natural audio geolocation, expanding the geolocation literature beyond ground/aerial imagery and urban acoustic sensing.

Comprehensive baseline comparison across multiple distinct paradigms: coordinate regression (Euclidean/Haversine), spatial classification (H3 hexagonal grids and hierarchical binning), explicit species range mapping, and multimodal retrieval.

Insightful diagnostic analysis with the 'Species Oracle' experiment, effectively framing the theoretical upper bound and illustrating how species co-occurrence patterns constrain geographic search space.
Introduction of the Xeno-Canto Dawn Chorus (XCDC) benchmark, highlighting the significant performance drop and open challenges of current models when exposed to species-dense acoustic environments.
Clear, structured writing with thorough appendix details covering location gallery design, classification grid trade-offs, and temporal aggregation.
weaknesses: Incremental methodological novelty: AG-CLIP is fundamentally an adaptation of GeoCLIP with an auxiliary multi-label BCE loss predicting precomputed SINR species checklists.

Marginal empirical gain from the proposed checklist auxiliary loss: as shown in Table 2b, adding the checklist loss provides essentially negligible improvement at city (6.4% vs 6.4%) and region (17.2% vs 17.0%) scales, and only modest gains at the continent scale (+2.7%). AG-CLIP's overall advantage over Hierarchical Classification (Table 1) is also narrow (1082 km vs 1117 km median error; 17.2% vs 16.6% region accuracy).

Unfair baseline comparison for audio representations: in Table 2a, Wav2CLIP and CLAP are evaluated frozen/off-the-shelf, whereas MobileNet-V3 is fine-tuned and pretrained specifically on iNatSounds. Evaluating or fine-tuning modern audio-specific transformers (e.g., AST, AudioMAE, BEATs, or fine-tuned CLAP) would provide a more rigorous comparison.

Heavy reliance of retrieval performance on test gallery construction: as shown in Table A1, using train/validation observation coordinates as the gallery gives substantially higher city accuracy (6.6%) compared to uniform geographic sampling (1.3%-2.9%), indicating that retrieval performance is heavily influenced by dataset density priors.
The multimodal geo-forensics application in Section 5.4 is purely anecdotal and qualitative, based on only four film scenes without quantitative validation or ground-truth verification.

strengths: Novel and compelling task formulation: While image geolocation has been extensively studied, global-scale audio geolocation—specifically leveraging natural soundscapes and wildlife vocalizations—is underexplored and presents a fresh research direction with clear utility for bioacoustics and geo-forensics.

Comprehensive benchmarking across paradigms: The paper methodically evaluates multiple formulation paradigms on the same benchmark, including direct coordinate regression (Euclidean and Haversine), hierarchical hexagonal grid classification (H3), retrieval against learned location encoders (GeoCLIP, SatCLIP, SINR), and species range intersections.

Insightful diagnostic and oracle analyses: The use of species checklists derived from SINR range maps provides an informative upper bound, demonstrating that knowing co-occurring species can theoretically localize sounds with high accuracy, while isolating the recall gap in current audio models.

Introduction of the XCDC dawn chorus benchmark and spatiotemporal aggregation: Evaluating multi-species dawn chorus recordings (XCDC) and testing spatiotemporal neighborhood pooling effectively reveals the current bottlenecks of single-clip models when confronting polyphonic, dense soundscapes.

Thorough ablations in the appendix: The manuscript includes detailed investigations into location gallery selection, audio backbones, variable-length temporal pooling, and the influence of pretraining datasets.
weaknesses: Modest algorithmic novelty: AG-CLIP mainly combines existing components (GeoCLIP contrastive framework, SINR range models, and standard MobileNet-V3 spectrogram backbones) with an auxiliary BCE loss predicting SINR checklists, rather than proposing a fundamentally new acoustic-spatial architecture.

Low fine-scale localization accuracy: Absolute geolocation accuracy from raw audio alone remains low at practical resolutions (only 6.4% within 25 km and 17.2% within 200 km on iNatSounds, dropping to 4.3% on XCDC), indicating that unconstrained audio geolocation remains largely unresolved without extensive aggregation.

Sensitivity to training geographic distribution: Table A1 shows that test performance drops substantially when using uniform global galleries rather than train-derived galleries (e.g., dropping from 17.4% to 15.0% at region level and 6.6% to 1.3% at city level), indicating that the retrieval mechanism relies heavily on the geographic sampling density of the training corpus.

Anecdotal geo-forensics evaluation: Section 5.4 introduces multimodal geo-forensics as a core contribution, but it is supported by only four cherry-picked Hollywood movie scenes without quantitative evaluation, error bounds, or statistical validation across a broader test suite.
